title: Merge Two Sorted Linked Lists
directAnswer: Use a dummy head and a tail pointer. Walk both lists; each step splice the smaller current node onto tail and advance that list and the tail. When one list empties, attach the entire remainder of the other in one link — it's already sorted. Return dummy.next. O(n + m) time, O(1) space, no new nodes.

remember.pattern: Dummy node + tail pointer two-pointer splice
remember.formula:
dummy = ListNode()
tail = dummy
while a and b:
    if a.val <= b.val: tail.next = a; a = a.next
    else: tail.next = b; b = b.next
    tail = tail.next
tail.next = a if a else b
return dummy.next
rules: Use a **dummy** head so the first splice uses the same code as every other — no `if head == null` branch.
Return `dummy.next`, never `dummy` — the dummy is a throwaway sentinel.
After the loop, attach the **remaining** list wholesale with one link: `tail.next = a or b`.
Use `<=` (not `<`) on ties to keep the merge **stable**; either is sorted, `<=` is conventional.
**Splice existing nodes** — don't allocate new ones — to stay O(1) space.
whenToUse: Merge two already-sorted singly linked lists into one sorted list
The merge step of merge sort on a linked list
Combining sorted streams where random access is unavailable
Building block for merging k sorted lists
antiSignals: Inputs are arrays with random access → index-based merge or a library sort may be simpler
You must merge many lists at once → use a min-heap (merge k sorted lists), not naive pairwise loops
Lists are unsorted → sort first; this assumes sorted inputs
You can't mutate the inputs → you'd copy nodes, costing O(n + m) space
remember.takeaway: The dummy-node + tail pattern strips every 'is this the first node?' edge case out of list building, and 'attach the sorted remainder in one link' avoids needless work. It's the backbone of merge k sorted lists, the merge phase of list merge sort, and Add Two Numbers.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you reach for a dummy head to avoid head-initialization edge cases and finish by splicing the leftover list in O(1) rather than node by node.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Writing tangled first-node logic without a dummy, or forgetting to attach the remaining list after the loop, dropping its nodes.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Use the dummy node, return dummy.next, splice the remainder in one assignment, and note this is exactly the merge step of merge sort and the building block of merge k sorted lists.

problemStatement:
You are given the heads of two sorted singly linked lists, `list1` and `list2`, each sorted in non-decreasing order.

Merge them into one **sorted** list by splicing together the existing nodes, and return *the head of the merged list*.
constraints: Both list1 and list2 are sorted in non-decreasing order
Either or both lists may be empty
understanding: Both inputs are sorted ascending. We weave their nodes into one ascending list, reusing existing nodes (splicing links) rather than allocating new ones. The dummy head removes the awkward 'what is the first node?' question.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are both lists guaranteed sorted in non-decreasing order?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — that precondition is what lets us merge in a single linear pass. Unsorted inputs would need a sort first.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I reuse the existing nodes or must I allocate new ones?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Splice the existing nodes for O(1) extra space. Allocating copies would waste O(n + m) memory for no benefit.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What if one or both lists are empty?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: If one is empty return the other; if both are empty return null. The dummy-node approach handles this with no special branch.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How are ties between equal values ordered?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Either order is still sorted. I'll take from list1 on ties using <= to keep the merge stable and predictable.

approaches.name: Iterative — Dummy Node + Tail Splice (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: Lead with this. The dummy node is the idiom interviewers want for list construction.
hints: You're building a new chain whose head you don't know until you compare the first two values. What if a fake node sat in front of the real head so the first append looks like every other append?
Keep a tail pointer starting on the dummy. Each step compare the two current heads, splice the smaller onto tail.next, advance that list, then advance tail.
When one list runs out, the other is already sorted — set tail.next to whichever list still has nodes, in one assignment, then return dummy.next.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each comparison advances one of the two pointers, so at most n + m iterations, each O(1). The leftover splice is one O(1) link. Only a dummy and a tail pointer are used → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
We assemble the merged list by always appending the smaller of the two current heads, anchored by a dummy sentinel.

**Why the dummy node.** Building a linked list normally forces an annoying special case: the *first* node has no predecessor to attach to, so you'd write `if (head == null) head = node; else tail.next = node;`. A dummy node placed before the real head means `tail` always has a valid `.next` to write — including the very first append. One uniform path, zero edge cases. The real list begins at `dummy.next`.

**The merge loop.** While both lists have nodes, compare `list1.val` and `list2.val`, splice the smaller node onto `tail.next`, advance that list's pointer, and move `tail` onto the node just attached. Using `<=` makes equal values take from `list1` first, keeping the merge stable.

**Why the leftover splice is O(1).** The loop exits the moment *one* list empties. The other is non-empty and already sorted and entirely ≥ everything appended so far (we always took the smallest available). So we don't iterate it — we point `tail.next` at its head and the whole tail comes along for free.

**Why we splice, not copy.** We rewire the `next` pointers of the original nodes instead of allocating new ones, keeping space at O(1) — the problem expects splicing the existing nodes.
approaches.insight: A dummy head turns 'build a list' into a branch-free loop, and 'attach the rest in one link' exploits the fact that a sorted remainder needs no further work. Together they are the entire merge phase of merge sort on linked lists.

approaches.name: Recursive — Pick Smaller Head, Recurse on the Rest
approaches.whenToMention: A clean alternative to mention; flag the O(n + m) call-stack cost versus the iterative O(1).
hints: If you knew the merge of the two tails, how would you build the full answer? Attach the smaller head in front of it.
Base cases: if either list is null, the merged result is simply the other list.
Otherwise compare the two heads; the smaller one's next becomes the merge of (its rest) with the other list, and you return that smaller head.
approaches.complexityReasoning: One recursive call consumes one node, so n + m calls total → O(n + m) time. The recursion depth equals the number of nodes → O(n + m) stack space.
approaches.explanation:
We define the merge in terms of itself: the merged list is the smaller of the two heads followed by the merge of everything else.

**Base cases first.** If `list1` is null, the merge is just `list2` (already sorted); symmetrically if `list2` is null. These stop the recursion and supply the tail of the final chain.

**The recursive step.** Compare the two heads. Say `list1.val <= list2.val`. Then `list1` is the smallest unused node, so it comes next: set `list1.next = merge(list1.next, list2)` — recursively merging the rest of list1 with all of list2 — and return `list1`. The mirror case handles `list2` being smaller.

**Why it's correct.** At every call the smallest remaining node across both lists is chosen as the local head, and by induction the recursive call correctly merges the strictly smaller remaining problem. The chain of returned heads is therefore globally sorted.

**The trade-off.** It reads beautifully and needs no dummy node, but each unmerged node adds a stack frame. On long lists (up to 5·10⁴ here) the iterative O(1)-space version avoids any stack-overflow risk — which is why it's the safer lead.
approaches.insight: Recursion expresses the merge as 'smallest head + merge of the rest', mirroring the iterative splice but offloading the bookkeeping to the call stack. Same O(n + m) time, but you trade O(1) space for O(n + m) frames.

pitfalls: Forgetting a base case — infinite recursion or a null dereference.
Returning the recursive result instead of the chosen head node.
Ignoring stack depth on long lists where the iterative version is safer.

commonMistakes: Skipping the dummy node and writing fragile first-node initialization logic.
Forgetting to attach the leftover list after the main loop, dropping nodes.
Returning the dummy node itself instead of dummy.next.
Allocating new nodes instead of splicing the existing ones.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Dropping the remaining list
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The loop exits as soon as one list empties; the other still has sorted nodes that must be spliced on. Omit this and you lose data.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Returning the dummy sentinel
commonMistakesDetailed.why: dummy holds a placeholder value (often 0). The real merged list begins at dummy.next; returning dummy prepends a bogus node.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
tail.next = list1 if list1 else list2
return dummy   # bogus leading node
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
tail.next = list1 if list1 else list2
return dummy.next

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Forgetting to advance the tail
commonMistakesDetailed.why: After tail.next = chosen, the next iteration writes tail.next again — overwriting the node you just attached unless you move tail forward first.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
if list1.val <= list2.val:
    tail.next = list1
    list1 = list1.next
# missing: tail = tail.next
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
if list1.val <= list2.val:
    tail.next = list1
    list1 = list1.next
tail = tail.next
